title: Landfall Bushwick — Editor Intro
summary: Editorial opening splash: the household reaches assigned shelter after intake; the city calls the case housed before the Vikings have inspected anything, and Carrie is already responsible for whatever they decide the room means.
settingText: Bushwick apartment building stairwell and fifth-floor landing, night
panelPlan: Full-page editorial/title splash. Use the cramped vertical stairwell as the dominant image: Carrie ahead with the brass key and thin DTI folder, the five displaced Norse adults climbing behind with bundled possessions. They should read as an exhausted adventuring party ascending rather than a static line of people on stairs.

Vary the party blocking: one person looking upward, one back down the stairwell, one resting briefly at a landing, Carrie already several steps ahead. The building is ordinary, worn, and much taller than anyone wants it to be.
Leave clean negative-space zones in walls and stairwell voids for the captions. The humor is that municipal paperwork has already declared success while everyone is still climbing.

dialogueInline.text: DTI calls this a successful placement.
dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION

dialogueInline.text: There is an address.
dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION

dialogueInline.text: There is a key.
dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION

dialogueInline.text: There are five flights of stairs.
dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION

dialogueInline.text: Carrie has explained that the fifth floor is not negotiable.
dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION

title: The Fifth-Floor Kingdom
summary: Carrie gets the household to 5B; the climb leaves them tired but alert, and Bjorn and Gunnar immediately judge the apartment as shelter rather than accepting Carrie's description of it.
settingText: Bushwick apartment building stairs and fifth-floor landing
panelPlan: Wide vertical stair composition: the group reaches the final flight looking genuinely weary. Carrie is at the fifth-floor landing with the key; Bjorn and Gunnar are still below her with the Kin distributed across the steps.
Medium at 5B: Carrie unlocks the door while Bjorn remains on the landing looking down the full stairwell they just climbed.
Wide into the studio from the doorway: Astrid and the two male Kin enter with bags while Gunnar stays at the threshold checking the hall, stair direction, and rear window visible beyond.
Two-shot Carrie/Bjorn at the door: she waits for his verdict; he gives her a logistical one instead of gratitude.
Final medium: Gunnar spots the fire escape through the rear window while Carrie is still trying to get everyone fully inside.

dialogueInline.text: Fifth floor. This is us.
There are four floors beneath us full of strangers.
That's usually how apartment buildings work.
And one stair.
There is a fire escape in back.
I saw it from the alley.
Of course you did.
If the lower stair is held, we leave by the rear iron.
If the building is on fire, yes.
Fire is one reason to leave quickly.
We're going to keep the list at fire.
For tonight.

title: One Room, Six Opinions
summary: The household occupies 5B immediately, making practical choices before Carrie can deliver a tour; Carrie's job becomes stopping only the choices that can damage the building or the placement.
panelPlan: Wide room geography: bare studio, kitchenette, radiator, window/fire escape, limited furniture. The household fans out immediately: Astrid at sink, Kin1 testing floor/wall for bedding, Kin2 testing window latch, Gunnar checking door swing and rear exit, Bjorn standing in the center taking the whole room in.
Medium: Carrie opens the DTI folder to begin her prepared orientation while nobody is facing her.
Medium: Kin1 starts moving a small table away from the wall; Carrie redirects only when it would block the entry door.
Medium: Gunnar tests the fire-escape window latch; Bjorn asks about the roof without looking at Carrie.
Wide: Carrie lowers the folder. The room is already changing around her.

dialogueInline.text: Okay. Before we start moving things—
Door needs the width.
More than that. It opens inward.
Yes. Great. Don't block the door.
Water works.
Window locks.
How do we reach the roof?
You don't.
There is a roof.
There are also sewers. You don't need to inspect the whole city tonight.
The rear window opens onto the iron stair.
Emergency use only.
You keep saying 'only' about useful things.
Because useful things become incident reports when you improvise.

title: Water in the Wall
summary: The household encounters running and hot water as an unexplained physical fact; Carrie can name parts of the system but cannot turn first-night astonishment into instant understanding.
panelPlan: Insert: Astrid turns the unfamiliar metal handle at the sink and water suddenly runs. Her hand stops in place; this is a first encounter, not routine appliance use.
Medium: Astrid tests the stream with her fingers, then turns the handle off and on once more to confirm that her action controls it.
Low medium: Gunnar crouches beneath the sink and follows the visible metal pipes into the wall without touching fittings or pretending to know their purpose.
Two-shot Bjorn/Carrie: Bjorn looks from the flowing water to the wall and asks the question that matters in his world: where is the source and who is moving it.
Wide: Carrie cannot give them a satisfying mechanical explanation. Astrid keeps the water running while the others continue unpacking around this impossible convenience.

dialogueInline.text: It comes when I turn this.
And leaves through that hole.
Yes. Sink, drain, pipes. Those are the names. I am not expecting any of this to mean anything yet.
Where is the well?
There isn't a well in the building.
Then who carries the water up here?
Nobody carries it.
Five floors.
I know.
Water does not climb because a woman turns a piece of metal.
That is an excellent objection and I cannot explain water pressure well enough to survive it.
The metal under here is warm.
That one brings hot water.
There is hot water in the wall.
Apparently that's the sentence we're ending on.

title: Emergency Provisions
summary: Carrie's emergency food is obviously insufficient; rather than march the entire household into the neighborhood, Carrie takes Bjorn and Gunnar to find food while Astrid and the two Kin stay behind in 5B.
panelPlan: Wide: Carrie empties the DTI emergency grocery bag onto the table: crackers, protein bars, bottled water, disposable utensils.
Medium on Bjorn looking at the food, then at the five displaced adults.
Medium: Gunnar checks the bag itself as though more food may be hidden in a seam.
Medium at the rear window: Gunnar smells food from the street below; outside, pigeons are visible on the iron structure beyond the window, but nobody comments on them yet.
Wide: Carrie puts her coat back on and deliberately takes only Bjorn and Gunnar. Astrid and the two male Kin remain in the apartment with the unpacked gear and nearly empty food bag.

dialogueInline.text: This is the food they sent with five people?
It was meant to get you through intake, not establish a winter hall.
It would not establish lunch.
Two bars. Six crackers. Water.
Your department prepares for hunger by making it measurable.
My department assumed I would get you somewhere with food.
There is food below us. Bread. Onions. Something frying.
There's a shop on the corner.
At night?
This is New York. Food is one of the things we're unusually good at.
We have silver.
Bring it. You and Gunnar are coming with me.
Astrid, I am not taking six people into one corner store.
We'll stay.

title: The Store Downstairs
summary: The first bodega transaction gives the household food but no useful understanding of modern money: Bjorn offers silver, Carrie performs an opaque card transaction, and Bjorn leaves knowing only that she paid a debt he intends to remember.
panelPlan: Wide: Carrie enters the compact bodega with Bjorn and Gunnar only. Ordinary customers continue shopping. The owner looks up once and goes back to work.

Medium: Carrie chooses basic groceries quickly. Bjorn judges recognizable food by sight; Gunnar compares objects, quantities and containers physically, turning packages in his hands and smelling produce.
Counter close: Bjorn places a small piece of hacksilver beside the groceries.
Two-shot owner/Carrie: the owner refuses the silver without ceremony. Carrie uses her modern payment card/terminal while Bjorn and Gunnar watch the unfamiliar exchange.
Medium: Bjorn watches the owner bag the food and watches Carrie's transaction complete; his concern is that Carrie has somehow paid, not how the mechanism works.
Close: the owner slides the hacksilver back to Bjorn.

dialogueInline.text: Door closes behind you.
For the food.
I can't take that.
It is silver.
I believe you. Still can't take it.
I'll pay.
With what?
This.
You touched a black thing to another black thing.
And now he has money.
I saw no money.
We're doing money on a different day.
How much did you give him?
Fifty-eight dollars and forty cents.
Then I owe you that.
You can owe me dinner by not starting a monetary theory before we eat it.
Take your silver.
You refuse good metal very calmly.
I get all kinds.

title: Dinner Was Already Underway
summary: Carrie, Bjorn and Gunnar return with groceries to discover that Second Male Kin used their absence to solve the food shortage himself: he has caught a pigeon from the exterior ironwork.
panelPlan: Wide from inside 5B: the door opens and Carrie, Bjorn and Gunnar return carrying grocery bags. Astrid and First Male Kin are arranging bedding and the room. Second Male Kin is at the rear window beside a bowl containing one very alive pigeon.
Medium: Carrie stops with the grocery bags still in her hands. Bjorn looks from the bags to the bird. Gunnar immediately notices the cord running out through the open window.
Medium on Second Male Kin: he explains the obvious logic—there were birds outside and the household needed food.
Two-shot Bjorn/Second Male Kin: Bjorn regards the successful catch as competent work, while Carrie is already walking toward the window to inspect where it happened.
Close on Carrie looking through the window and seeing that the cord has been rigged across part of the exterior iron landing toward the neighboring section.

dialogueInline.text: Why is there a pigeon in a bowl?
For dinner.
We brought dinner.
Now there is more.
You caught it here?
Birds sit on the iron outside. I had cord.
You made a snare on that?
It worked.
Quickly.
They are not cautious birds.
Nobody touch the pigeon for one minute.
It has already been touched.
Then nobody improve the situation while I look at it.

title: The Second Road
summary: Carrie explains what the exterior ironwork is for only because the Kin have already used it for something else; Bjorn accepts that the snare is badly placed without accepting that catching pigeons is itself unreasonable.
settingText: Bushwick studio main window and fire escape
panelPlan: Wide at the rear window: Carrie leans out just enough to inspect the exterior iron landing. Second Male Kin shows where he tied the snare. Gunnar studies the iron stairs physically from inside the window.
Medium: Carrie points down the connected iron flights and explains that people use them to escape if the interior stair cannot be used.
Medium on Bjorn looking down the route to the ground, immediately understanding it as a second road out of the room.
Medium on Second Male Kin: he looks at the cord crossing part of that route and concedes the placement problem, not the hunting premise.
Wide: Second Male Kin frees the pigeon and removes the cord from their section. Unknown to them, a separate loose end remains beyond the neighboring window.

dialogueInline.text: This ironwork is for getting people out if the stairs inside cannot be used.
It reaches the ground.
That's the idea. The city calls it a fire escape.
Then it is a second road from the room.
A narrow one.
No one was using it.
When they need it, they need it immediately.
Then the snare was badly placed.
Yes. And there are no snares on the fire escape.
Those are two judgments.
I am making both.
The bird is still food.
The bird is leaving.

title: Dinner Announces Itself
summary: After the pigeon is released, the household cooks the groceries; the unfamiliar stove and smoke alarm create a second first-night collision with modern domestic technology.
panelPlan: Wide: Astrid examines the unfamiliar stove while Carrie demonstrates one control once. Second Male Kin is visibly empty-handed after losing the pigeon; the grocery bags are now open on the counter.
Medium: flame or burner heat appears from the stove. Astrid immediately understands the practical result even though the mechanism is alien.
Wide: cooking begins. A little smoke rises higher than expected.
Large reaction panel: the smoke alarm suddenly SHRIEKS. Bjorn and Gunnar react physically to an unexplained alarm while Carrie grabs a towel and clears smoke beneath it.
Medium: everyone looks up at the small ceiling device after it quiets; it has acquired a purpose through experience, not explanation.

dialogueInline.text: Turn this. The fire comes from here.
Without wood.
Without wood.
BEEP! BEEP! BEEP! BEEP!
dialogueInline.speaker: SFX

dialogueInline.text: Nobody hit the ceiling. It's warning us about the smoke.
We can see the smoke.
The thing on the ceiling cannot.
Then how does it know?
It senses smoke.
But does not know there is smoke.
You have found the philosophical weakness of the smoke alarm.
The pigeon would have smoked less.
The pigeon is gone.
Exactly.

title: The Neighbor Has the Other End
summary: The upstairs neighbor arrives with the length of Second Male Kin's snare that reached her window; the household learns the exterior iron is shared space because an actual neighbor claims her part of it.
panelPlan: Wide: knock at 5B. Upstairs Neighbor stands in the hall holding a separate length of cord she removed from beside her window. Carrie opens the door; Second Male Kin is visible behind her and recognizes it immediately.
Medium: Neighbor holds the cord out. Second Male Kin explains where he tied it, revealing that his idea of the household boundary extended too far.
Medium: Carrie gives a direct apology. Astrid appears with one unopened spicy packaged snack from the bodega bag.
Close: Astrid offers the snack; Neighbor takes it after a beat without becoming friendly.
Wide: Neighbor walks away with the problem settled only provisionally. Carrie closes the door while Second Male Kin looks at the now-returned cord in his hand.

dialogueInline.text: This was tied next to my window.
I tied it to the iron beside ours.
It crossed mine.
I did not know that part was yours.
The part outside my window is mine enough.
It's down now, and it stays down. I'm sorry.
For trouble.
What is it?
Spicy.
I'll take it.
The bird was released.
There was a bird?
Briefly.
Keep it that way.

title: Witnessed
summary: Carrie uses DTI's routine witnessed-mark procedure for an applicant who cannot read the acknowledgement; there is no procedural crisis because this is ordinary work for a temporal-displacement department.
panelPlan: Wide: the household continues settling 5B while Carrie clears a corner of the table and opens the placement acknowledgement.
Medium: Carrie reads the operative placement terms aloud to Bjorn, then places a small ink pad beside the witnessed-mark field without hesitation.
Two-shot: Bjorn asks what his mark will mean; Carrie explains the procedure as something she already knows and has used before.
Close: Bjorn presses his thumb into the ink and then into the witnessed-mark field.
Medium: Carrie signs the witness attestation beside his thumbprint and closes that part of the packet.

dialogueInline.text: I have to record that I read you the placement terms and that you agreed to them.
I cannot read the page.
I know. That's why this box exists.
I read it aloud. You tell me whether you agree. If you do, you leave a mark here and I sign beside it saying I witnessed the agreement.
And if I do not agree?
Then you don't make the mark and I write down what you object to.
That is an honest arrangement.
No knife?
Nobody is bleeding on my forms.
Then ink will do.
Placement acknowledged. One thing tonight has gone exactly the way it is supposed to.

title: The Other Mark
summary: The routine witnessed mark prompts Bjorn to ask where the building owner's obligations are recorded; Carrie knows the answer, but the word 'landlord' opens a conceptual door she cannot close.
panelPlan: Close: Carrie's signature sits beside Bjorn's thumbprint.
Two-shot: Bjorn points from his mark to Carrie's witness signature and asks about the absent other party.
Medium: Carrie pulls the lease/placement papers closer and explains that the building owner has his own agreement and obligations.
Medium on Gunnar listening while he coils the confiscated cord; he does not inspect the writing.
Close on Bjorn as Carrie says the ordinary modern word 'landlord.'

dialogueInline.text: Your mark says you heard me agree.
It says I witnessed it.
Where is the mark of the man who owns this place?
On the lease. Different document.
What does he agree to?
That if the tenancy is in good standing, he provides the apartment and maintains the things the law requires him to maintain.
So he has terms too.
Absolutely. DTI does not put people in rooms where only the tenant has obligations.
What do you call the owner?
The landlord.
Landlord.

title: What Can Take It Away
summary: Bjorn asks what can actually cost them the room; Carrie gives a competent, practical answer, and the household realizes the fire-escape snare is a real risk rather than a paperwork technicality.
settingText: Bushwick studio table / phone on speaker
panelPlan: Medium at the table: Bjorn asks what can actually end a temporary placement.
Two-shot: Carrie answers from professional knowledge, distinguishing ordinary confusion from actual safety, damage, or conduct problems.
Reaction panel: Second Male Kin looks toward the returned snare cord beside his gear.
Medium: Carrie follows his eyeline and names the relevant problem without turning it into a lecture.
Close on Bjorn: the useful fact he takes away is that removal requires an actual reason, not that he has mastered housing law.

dialogueInline.text: You keep calling the room temporary. What ends it?
Review can change the placement. So can serious damage, violence, blocking an exit, repeated safety problems, or refusing conditions that actually matter.
Not knowing what the water in the wall is.
DTI would have no clients left if confusion were disqualifying.
The cord was on one of the ways out.
That is why I cared about the cord more than the pigeon.
It was removed.
Which is why you're still having this conversation in the room instead of downstairs with me explaining it to Housing.
Then they need a reason to take the room.
A real one.
Useful.

title: Land. Lord.
summary: Carrie's ordinary use of 'landlord' maps perfectly onto Bjorn's political vocabulary; the more accurately she describes tenancy, the more convinced he becomes that modern people have simply kept lordship and changed the paperwork.
panelPlan: Medium: Carrie puts the completed acknowledgement aside and begins gathering the rest of the placement papers.
Two-shot: Bjorn returns to the word landlord and tests it against the few facts he now knows: ownership, payment, shelter, and enforceable obligations.
Medium: Carrie rejects the comparison while answering concrete questions because those questions are legitimate.
Medium on Gunnar, listening to the argument rather than reading any document.
Close on Bjorn, satisfied that Carrie's objections have not changed the structure as he sees it.

dialogueInline.text: You call him the land-lord because he owns the land.
It's one word, and he is not a lord.
Does he own the building?
Yes.
Do we give him payment to remain in it?
Rent.
Can he try to remove us if we break the agreement?
Through an actual legal process, yes.
And if he fails his agreement?
Then tenants have remedies against him too.
So both sides can accuse the other of failing.
Now you're closer.
A lord with obligations is still a lord.
That conclusion was not hidden inside anything I said.
It did not need to be.

title: Not About the Form
summary: Carrie's supervisor confirms the routine witnessed mark without drama and immediately moves to the real first-night problem: building management has reported the fire-escape snare.
panelPlan: Medium: Carrie's phone rings while she is closing the completed placement packet; the thumbprint and witness attestation are already finished.
Two-shot: the supervisor confirms receipt in one sentence and makes clear the call is about something else.
Medium: Carrie stands and looks toward the rear window as the fire-escape complaint is described.
Medium on Bjorn, who can hear the words animal snare and believes factual precision is helping.
Close on Carrie as the supervisor reminds her that repeated building-safety complaints can jeopardize the placement.

dialogueInline.text: I have the packet. Witnessed mark is fine. I'm calling about the building.
I was afraid you might be.
Management reported an obstruction on the rear fire escape.
Removed immediately. No injury, no damage, neighbor spoken to.
The report says 'animal snare.'
It caught the animal.
That fact is not helping the placement.
Was that Bjorn?
That was one of the five adults I am currently preventing from improving the official record.
One more building-safety complaint and Housing can request reassessment.
Then there won't be one.
There should not have been one this time. The neighbor was compensated.
She received a spicy snack.
I'm going to let you handle that sentence.

title: The Brass Key
summary: Carrie hands over the single apartment key; Bjorn understands the lock immediately and values the privacy far more than the paperwork that produced it.
panelPlan: Insert: scratched brass key in Carrie's palm.
Close: Bjorn takes it and turns it once between thumb and forefinger.
Two-shot at the door: Carrie demonstrates the deadbolt only as much as needed; Bjorn tests the lock himself.
Medium: Gunnar points out that one key is a bottleneck for six adults.
Close: Bjorn closes his hand around the key.

dialogueInline.text: One key tonight. Copies tomorrow.
One key for six people is a poor arrangement.
For once, your complaint is completely normal.
From inside, the door answers to us.
Once it's locked, the door answers to you.
And from outside, the key decides.
That's a lock.
An excellent invention.
Until the person with the only key leaves.
Tomorrow we make six.
Tomorrow a locksmith makes copies. You make nothing.
Then tomorrow the locksmith proves useful.

directionInline.text: Use the same ordinary scratched brass apartment key established throughout the issue.

title: The Landlord
summary: Carrie explains rent only as an oral exchange of obligations; Bjorn maps it onto lordship because that is the political structure he actually knows, while modern tenancy remains mostly opaque.
panelPlan: Medium: Carrie, Bjorn and Gunnar at the table after the key handoff. Carrie explains the arrangement aloud using the room around them.
Two-shot: Carrie points to roof, running water, locked door and the unfamiliar heat source as things the building owner must maintain.
Medium: Gunnar counts the obligations on his fingers.
Close on Bjorn reaching the lordship conclusion with complete seriousness.
Two-shot Carrie/Bjorn: she realizes the explanation has made his opinion more entrenched.

dialogueInline.text: You pay each month to stay here. The owner has to keep the roof sound, the water coming, the door working, and the heat on.
So we pay him and he keeps the hall fit to live in.
That's the basic deal.
Roof. Water. Door. Heat.
And if one fails?
Then he has failed his side of it.
So the payment binds him too.
Yes. That part matters.
He owns the building. We pay him. He owes protection of the roof and heat.
I know where you're going.
He is our lord.
He is not your lord.
You have described a lord with monthly billing.
I have described a landlord.
Exactly.

title: Their Order
summary: The household arranges 5B by familiar physical logic; Carrie's interventions reveal unfamiliar building rules only when somebody actually collides with one.
panelPlan: Wide: Astrid claims food/cooking shelf; Kin1 selects dry bedding area; Kin2 arranges small tools; Gunnar preserves the main door path; Bjorn proposes a central shared-gear area.
Medium: Kin1 rejects Bjorn's preferred bedding placement because of a draft and moves his bundle himself.
Medium: Kin2 hangs a heavy wet item from an exposed ceiling pipe simply because the pipe is strong and well placed.
Fast intervention: Carrie removes the item and points to the small sprinkler head, explaining only the immediate consequence.
Wide: the room arrangement continues; the unfamiliar ceiling device has acquired one terrifying fact and nothing more.

dialogueInline.text: Shared gear here. Bedding on that wall.
Draft comes through there.
Then move it.
Take that off the pipe.
It is strong.
It is connected to something that can dump water over the entire room.
From that little piece?
If there's a fire.
Another thing in the building that waits for fire.
This building has thought about fire more than all of us combined.
Food stays here.
Nothing blocks the door.
And nothing hangs from the ceiling water trap.
I am not correcting the name. I just want you to leave it alone.

title: The Iron Thing Knocks
summary: The old radiator makes an unexplained noise; Carrie can name it and say it provides heat, but Bjorn and Gunnar remain at the level of immediate physical observation rather than understanding boilers, valves or building systems.
panelPlan: Insert at floor level: the old cast-iron radiator gives a sudden metallic knock and vibrates slightly.
Medium: Bjorn and Gunnar both turn sharply toward the unexplained noise; Gunnar crouches near the iron object but does not manipulate it.
Two-shot Carrie/Gunnar: Carrie names it as a radiator and says the noise is ordinary.
Medium: Bjorn holds a hand near the warm metal, testing the only fact he can verify.
Wide: everyone returns to settling the room while Gunnar remains suspicious of an object that is warm and knocks by itself.

dialogueInline.text: KONK.
dialogueInline.speaker: SFX

dialogueInline.text: That iron thing struck itself.
Radiator. It makes noise when the heat comes through.
What comes through?
Heat. Hot water or steam. I genuinely do not know which this building uses.
You live in this city and do not know what is inside the thing that warms your room.
I know enough not to open it.
That is not the same knowledge.
No, and tonight it is the safer kind.
It is warm.
That's the part we're keeping.
And the knocking?
We're keeping that too. Apparently.

title: If Something Happens
summary: Carrie tries to leave emergency instructions and is forced to confront how little first-night infrastructure the household can actually use: they cannot read her contact card or operate a phone, so the practical plan becomes finding a known modern person.
settingText: Bushwick studio table near the door
panelPlan: Insert: Carrie starts writing emergency/contact numbers on a card out of habit.
Medium: she looks at the card, then at the five Vikings, and realizes the card is useless to them tonight.
Medium: Carrie holds up her phone briefly while asking whether anyone knows how to use one; their expressions answer before they do.
Two-shot: Carrie substitutes a human plan—if there is immediate trouble, go to the food shop downstairs or the neighbor and ask them to summon help.
Medium: Bjorn accepts the chain of people more readily than the unexplained device.

dialogueInline.text: If something happens after I leave, these are the numbers—
Right. None of you can read this.
I told you that.
And none of you knows how to use this.
The black glass you keep speaking into.
That's enough identification for one day.

New plan. If there is fire, get out. If somebody is badly hurt or something happens that you cannot handle, go downstairs to the food merchant or knock on the neighbor's door. Tell them to summon help.
The merchant is now part of your government.
Tonight the merchant is part of me getting to go home.
That is a large responsibility for a man who sells onions.
He has no idea.

title: Incident Report
summary: Carrie files the required report aloud enough for the household to object to her version; they cannot read the record, which makes their insistence on oral precision even more irritating.
panelPlan: Medium: Carrie sits at the table typing an incident report while the household settles around her.
Close on Carrie as she quietly dictates or reads back the factual sentence she is entering: obstruction removed, animal unharmed, neighbor notified.
Medium: Second Male Kin hears the wording and objects to the omission that the snare functioned; Bjorn supports the distinction from nearby.
Two-shot: Carrie explains that the purpose of the report is not to celebrate the quality of the snare.
Wide: Carrie continues typing as the household prepares for sleep.

dialogueInline.text: 'Cord removed from exterior stair. Animal released unharmed. Neighbor notified.'
You left out that the snare worked.
Intentionally.
A failed snare and a successful snare are different facts.
The fact DTI cares about is that there was a trap where people flee a burning building.
That is the location of the mistake.
I am not submitting 'excellent snare, unfortunate venue.'
It would be more accurate.
The accurate outcome is that you still have housing when I finish typing.
Then include that.
That part goes in my prayers.

title: Carrie's Excellent Placement
summary: The DTI supervisor calls about the incident; Carrie defends the placement as safe and corrected while the Vikings' audible commentary makes her case progressively harder to present as routine.
panelPlan: Medium: phone on speaker, Carrie seated at table with completed placement paperwork and incident report.
Medium on Carrie as supervisor lists the complaint facts in bureaucratic language.
Medium on Bjorn and Gunnar nearby, listening as though this is a review of their work.
Two-shot Carrie/Bjorn as she tries to keep him out of the call.
Close on Carrie after the supervisor reminds her the placement is under her supervision.

dialogueInline.text: First night: obstruction of required egress, animal trapping, neighbor complaint.
Corrected before the complaint reached us. No injury. No damage. Egress is clear.
You were on site.
I was standing three feet from it.
The placement is under your supervision.
I am aware of the sentence you are building.
Tell him the neighbor accepted compensation.
She accepted a spicy snack.
Compensation.
Was that him again?
I have five adults in one room and no private office. Everybody is 'him again.'
One more building-safety complaint and Housing can request reassessment.
Then I'll keep Housing out of it.
We also understand.
You understand nothing until I hang up.

title: Tomorrow's Orders
summary: Carrie leaves a short set of concrete prohibitions framed in things the Vikings can actually identify after one day, while Gunnar finds the one unmentioned direction: up.
panelPlan: Wide: Carrie stands near the door putting on her coat; the household is now functional but still sparse.
Medium: Carrie gives a short overnight prohibition list framed in physical things everyone has actually encountered that day.
Reaction on Second Male Kin as hunting from the exterior iron is explicitly forbidden; he accepts the restriction without embarrassment.
Two-shot Carrie/Bjorn: he observes the rule list has grown rapidly.
Close on Gunnar looking upward toward the ceiling after Carrie finishes, already finding the unmentioned direction.

dialogueInline.text: Until morning: no hunting from the building. Leave the iron stairs outside alone. Do not open anything attached to the walls, floor or ceiling. Do not make a fire indoors. If somebody knocks, answer without a weapon in your hand.
You made a long law from a short evening.
You gave me excellent source material.
The bird was one event.
The bird already has paperwork.
You said nothing about above us.
The roof is also part of the building.
But not inside it.
I can hear tomorrow becoming worse.
Then sleep before it arrives.

title: Lock It Behind Me
summary: Carrie finally leaves; the key gives the household privacy, but the last exchange makes clear she is not leaving them wiser—only temporarily contained.
settingText: Bushwick studio doorway and fifth-floor hallway
panelPlan: Wide: Carrie stands in open doorway with coat and folder; household remains inside among bedding, groceries, tools and map.
Medium: Bjorn follows to threshold with brass key.
Close: Carrie points to the key and then the lock.
Hallway two-shot: she steps outside; Bjorn remains inside.
Insert from inside: brass key turns, deadbolt locks.
Wide interior: Bjorn tests the handle. Gunnar sits with the map, already looking upward; the others continue settling.

dialogueInline.text: Lock the door behind me.
You cannot enter without the key.
That is the dream.
You are responsible for us but cannot enter our room.
That's how privacy works.
Your government has finally produced a sensible arrangement.
Good night, Bjorn.
Good night, Carrie.
She forbade the iron stairs.
She did.
She did not forbid looking out the window.

title: Landfall
summary: The household ends its first modern night with only a handful of things understood through direct experience: the door locks, water comes from the wall, the iron heater is warm and noisy, food can be bought downstairs, and the roof remains unknown.
panelPlan: Wide interior: temporary bedding arranged; groceries, completed packet, contact card Carrie started but did not leave as usable instructions, and bundled Norse gear coexist. The room is functional, not cozy.
Medium: Astrid stores food; Kin1 checks bedding; Kin2 checks the window latch. No one waits for Bjorn to assign tasks.
Medium on Bjorn: brass key on a simple hook. He looks from it to the sink and the warm iron radiator, still treating both as unresolved facts rather than understood systems.
Medium on Gunnar at the window, looking up toward the roofline without climbing outside.
Exterior hallway: Carrie pauses outside the locked door, reads a new DTI message on her phone, grimaces, and heads toward the stairs.

dialogueInline.text: Food is away.
Bedding stays dry here.
The window holds.
The door locks. Water comes when we ask for it. The iron thing is warm.
And strikes itself.
We have not solved that.
Tomorrow I need to know where north is.
Then find north.
Higher would help.
Sleep would help more.
Oh, come on.
